Session title: Lunch & Sponsor Booths
Women's Leadership in the AI Era
Full description:
AI did not suddenly make accomplished women less capable. But it has introduced an entirely new vocabulary for skills many women leaders already use every day.

Giving clear direction became prompt engineering. Building repeatable processes became workflows. Providing context, managing ambiguity, asking better questions, and exercising judgment became the foundations of effective AI leadership.

So why do so many accomplished women still feel behind?

In this fireside conversation, Leah Russo, Vice President of Marketing at Clearco, and Allison Moore, CEO of Chief, will examine what the AI transition is revealing about confidence, credibility, experimentation, and who feels entitled to claim expertise.

They’ll explore the difference between learning genuinely new technology and recognizing the value of capabilities women have spent years developing. They’ll also discuss how leaders can create the psychological safety people need to experiment before they feel confident, and how to ensure AI reduces the burden of leadership instead of becoming one more thing women are expected to master.

This is not a conversation about becoming more technical or keeping up with every new tool. It is about learning the technology without allowing unfamiliar terminology to erase the evidence of your existing competence.

Attendees will leave with a clearer understanding of:

• Why feeling behind is not always the same as being behind
• Which leadership skills become more valuable as AI handles more execution
• How to build credibility when everyone is still learning
• Why experimentation must come before confidence
• How to use AI to create leverage and reduce mental load

Most importantly, they’ll leave with a more useful question than “Do I know enough?”

What am I ready to try next?
Short summary: What AI Is Revealing About Women, Leadership, and Expertise

Session title: Afternoon Break
Navigating Bias and Difficult Conversations
Full description:
Women in executive GTM roles are outperforming their male peers on quota attainment and still being passed over for promotion, watching their ideas get credited to someone else in pipeline reviews, and receiving feedback that says "polish" when no one will say plainly what they mean. A 2024 global survey of 5,000 women found the most common reason women do not report bias is
not fear of retaliation — it is that they concluded the behavior was not serious enough. A 2026 peer-reviewed study confirmed that men consistently prefer women leaders who reinforce the status quo over those who advocate for equity. The bias is structural, the cost is real, and the gap is a practical one: women need language precise enough to name what happened, an ask specific enough to move, and a peer in their corner before they walk into the room. This session delivers all three.

• Separate common themes from signals that are new, accelerating, or changing
• Turn buyer language into stronger positioning, campaigns, and GTM decisions
• Build prompts that make AI show its work

Nick Mehta: Nick Mehta most recently explored agentic startup ideas as an Entrepreneur-in-Residence at Bessemer Venture Partners and as an advisor at Chemistry Ventures, after handing off the CEO role at Gainsight to his President and successor.

Prior to that, he spent 12.5 years co-founding and serving as CEO of Gainsight, the iconic company that defined the category of Customer Success for SaaS companies. Under Nick's leadership, the company scaled to $235M in Annual Recurring Revenue and $60M+ EBITDA. During its Venture Capital-backed era from 2013 to 2020, Gainsight raised $150M from top software investors including Battery Ventures, Bain Capital Ventures, Bessemer Venture Partners, Lightspeed Venture Partners, Insight Venture Partners and Salesforce Ventures. At the end of 2020, Vista Equity Partners acquired Gainsight for $1.1B in an all-cash transaction.

Gainsight championed the new role of Customer Success Management to help businesses maximize Net Revenue Retention. The Customer Success Manager (CSM) population in the world grew from a few thousand in 2013 to hundreds of thousands by 2025. Gainsight helped evangelize the category by publishing five books with Wiley Publishing on the topic, including 4 co-authored by Nick. Gainsight ran hundreds of Customer Success events, including the industry-standard conference, Pulse, which grew to thousands of attendees annually across the US and Europe.

Gainsight earned recognition for its world-class culture. Gainsight's 1100+ employees across the US, Canada, the UK, EMEA, India and Japan were passionate about its mission: "to be living proof you can win in business, while being Human-First." In 2023, it was recognized as the #1 Best Place to Work across all company sizes by Glassdoor.

Gainsight was a five-time Forbes Cloud 100 recipient. Nick was named the #2 CEO by the Software Report, had a 98% approval rating on Glassdoor and won the Enterpreneur of the Year Award for Northern California.

Prior to Gainsight, Nick was the CEO of Summit Partners-backed LiveOffice, which he sold to Symantec and he later served as a VP/GM at Symantec. He even co-founded a failed 1990s golf startup from his dorm room, which you should ask him about some time. He'll show you their hilarious dotcom commercial and you can ask where the venture capital dollars went.

In addition to his full-time roles, Nick serves on the boards of F5 (NASDAQ: FFIV), PubMatic (NASDAQ: PUBM), Gainsight, and the a16z-backed AI measurement company Larridin. Nick also co-founded the non-profit New Work Foundation to help young people navigate their careers in the world of AI.

Nick earned his Bachelor's in Biochemical Sciences Magna Cum Laude from Harvard College and Master's in Computer Science from Harvard University.

Outside of work, Nick is passionate about family, physics, philosophy, fiction, pop music and his Pittsburgh Steelers. People say there is no way to connect all of those interests with business, but he continues to try.

On a closing note, Nick's Indian-American mom would like to point out that he still has time to become a doctor.
